utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi and Daryl Mundis, assisted by our case manager, Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Mundis. Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President, good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stefane Bourgon co-counsel, and our Alex Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom and around the courtroom assisting us in our task. We will be continuing with the hearing of the witness who started with his testimony yesterday. Defence counsel have 15 questions left to put to the witness. I thought they needed 15 minutes, but in fact they need to put 15 additional questions to the witness. I will now ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, it might be useful if there is a witness who is testifying for a one-day period, to be prepared in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I just want to make sure that everything is functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you well now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber greets you and will now give the floor to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and good day, Mr. Menzil.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you were saying that you visited the civilians who were placed in the gym in the school in Mehurici. You said you did everything to ensure that the conditions they were in was as good as possible. And you also took certain sanitary measures to prevent any diseases from spreading. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell me whether you received any wounded men on that day, and given the fighting, can you remember how many wounded and dead there were in your clinic, if there were any?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday I was saying that I visited the civilians in the sports hall for a brief period of time, because there was very fierce fighting and there were wounded men who kept arriving. On that day, 69 wounded were treated, most of whom were very seriously wounded. There were quite a lot of wounds caused by trip mines, and then there were wounds that were the result of various other weapons. I didn't spend that much time up there. I spent more time in the reception centre, apart from when I went to the place up there and visited them, apart from the 69 wounded, there were nine individuals who had been killed and who had been brought to my reception centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menzil, on that day, that night, did you receive any wounded members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, towards the end of the day, when the fighting was no longer that intense, I assume it was about 8.00 in the evening, two members of the HVO in uniform were brought to me by members of the ABiH. I'm not sure who they were, but I could see that they were members of the ABiH, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And since at the time I was treating one of our wounded, when these two HVO members were brought in, one of them was very seriously wounded, so I postponed the treatment of our wounded man, because the member of the HVO, one of the HVO members, was seriously wounded. We treated him. We did what was possible for us to do then, gave him a drip. And as far as the second wounded HVO member is concerned, he was not so seriously wounded. He was only lightly wounded. When I saw how seriously the other HVO member was wounded, I went to the hospital in Zenica with an escort with him. The Mehurici-Zenica road that went by Ovnak was cut off, had been unblocked at the time, so it was easier to reach the hospital. I noticed that the wounded man I've been talking about had been hit by a number of bullets in the peripheral and frontal areas of his body. It was also necessary to give him stitches to stop the bleeding. And although he was able to communicate, he was conscious, you could see that he was very frightened, depressed. So I personally escorted him. I handed him over to Dr. Ana in the hospital in Zenica. She was from Kotor Varos. And since the wounded man said that he would like some members of the clergy to be informed of his condition, I suggested that Ana contact members of the clergy from the hospital in Zenica, and she did that in my presence. I think his name was Zoran or Darko. I'm not sure, though. He was a young man, about 19 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Menzil, please tell me: When you returned on the following day, or later on, did you notice that, apart from the civilians who were in the gym, did you notice that there were HVO members who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, after combat had ended on that day, we, as members of the command, because I was a member of the battalion command, I was a medical corps officer, we took stock of the situation, of everything that had happened that day, and we reported from our respective fields at that briefing, at that meeting which took place in the evening, around midnight. I found out that a certain group of HVO members were located somewhere in Mehurici and on the following day I found out the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menzil, did you visit them and what sort of a state were they in?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since they were HVO members and, naturally, the battalion commander made the suggestion, it was my duty to go and see what sort of condition these people were in. They were in a room. I'm not from Mehurici. I'm from Kotor Varos. So I don't know what that room was used for before. But it was not very comfortable. But at that moment in time, it was the most appropriate room they had for providing accommodation for, let's say, the enemy side. This was for the sake of their physical protection and because this area could be protected from extremists who might want to break in and threaten these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menzil, tell me: Who was providing security for the people who were in the sports hall, and who was providing security for the HVO detainees?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the civilian MUP provided security for the people in the hall, and sports hall, and in this room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I put two questions to you, in fact. When you visited the HVO members, what sort of condition were they in in terms of their health? Did you have to treat them or rather did they complain about maltreatment by those who were guarding them? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first time I visited them, that was the second day after they had been detained. The first time I saw them was to see what sort of physical condition they were in. I wanted to see whether there were any wounded men, whether it was necessary to evacuate, or rather, to transfer some of them to the hospital, given the physical condition they were in at the time. They seemed depressed, afraid. Yet when I spoke to them, when I observed them, I didn't notice any wounded men among them. But one of them did complain about high blood pressure and said that he had been receiving treatment, but at that moment, at that point in time, he didn't have any medicine. I mentioned this problem to a doctor who was there, Dr. Ribic, and we managed to provide this man with a certain form of treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, tell me: Did the International Red Cross visit the people in the hall and the HVO members during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A few days later, the International Red Cross appeared on the scene. I don't know whether it's necessary to say that there was a minor incident involving the Arabs when the International Red Cross appeared, they tried to take the flags off the vehicles and erase the symbols of the International Red Cross, but the Red Cross did visit the people in the hall, and they also visited the detained HVO members. They spoke to them. As to what they spoke about, I don't know, but the Red Cross did visit them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And by last question --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Menzil: When you look back to the conditions that prevailed in June 1993, would you say that you did everything to secure and protect the people who were kept in the sports hall, and did you do the same for the detained HVO members? Did you do everything that you could for them at the time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that I have already spoken about this, but when I look back to the situation at the time, I think we did all we could, in terms of medical care, in particular. Given the conditions that prevailed at the time, I don't think we could have done anything more for any of them at the time. I don't think we could have provided them with better conditions. I don't know what else we could have done, apart from all things that I have mentioned. Perhaps I have forgotten to mention that the people in the sports hall were provided with beds, so none of them had to sleep on the floor. Some of the soldiers also gave them their sleeping bags. I've also mentioned the food that was provided. They were provided with the necessary sanitary conditions, medical, or rather, hygienic items, soap, washing powder, warm water, hot water, that is. And as far as these other members are concerned, I think there were about 15 of them. We did everything that we could to provide them with decent conditions and to treat them in accordance with the military code of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. President, this concludes my examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The other Defence team, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this moment, we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm turning towards the Prosecution, and I'm giving them the floor for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First we would like to distribute just a few -- two documents which I may or may not use during the cross-examination, just for your convenience, Mr. President. One is a copy of a map, which the gentleman might use to show us where he was, and the second one, a document which I might discuss at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just -- I'd just like to clarify a few of the points you made yesterday and today so we understand a little bit more what happened during these days. And it's really clarification of the points you made. Let me just start with what you just talked about. That was these detention or whatever we want to call it, of HVO people in one place and the women, children in the other place, in the gym. And I believe that incidents occurred after the 8th of June, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The incidents themselves were preceded by the specific situation that I spoke about yesterday, and this situation culminated towards the end of April and escalated in -- towards the end of May. And this was the blockade of roads and frequent provocations. At the end of this, there was a blockade of a settlement called Velika Bukovica, where all the civilians were. On several occasions, they sent a courier to the unit that I belonged to, asking for our assistance. They wanted assistance, they wanted help. There was even some alarming reports about people having been killed and burnt already. And when you say "incidents," what do you mean, sir? What do you say when you say after the 8th? What incidents are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I want to talk about the detention of these people, the women and children in the gym, and the HVO soldiers in that room you talked about. These detentions occurred after the events of the 8th of June, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to hear what the Defence has to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend is using the word "detainees" or he says that these people were detained. As far as I can remember, the person never spoke about the civilians being detained. He said that they were accommodated in the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's fine, whatever words you want to describe for pulling people into a room. That's fine. We can use "accommodated." That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But let me talk about the date. When did that sequence of events start? It started on the 8th of June, 1993; is that correct? That the people were put together, accommodated, into these two locations?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned that that evening, I believe, there was a meeting at the brigade -- at the battalion command of -- and I assume you were present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was very late, around midnight, after the end of those combat activities, when those combat activities subsided to a certain extent. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was present at that meeting, apart from you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other members of the command, the battalion commander was there as well, and I can't remember the names of all those who were present. In any case, those were people who were members of the command of the battalion at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And at that time, the battalion was called the 1st Siprage Battalion, or was it already part of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Yesterday I said that the Siprage Detachment existed until the 22nd of December. On the 25th December, it became the 1st Battalion, 306th mountain brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And incidentally, at what time was it transformed into the 27th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on that evening, during that meeting of the battalion command, who was the battalion commander who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've already asked me that. It was Mr. Mirza Lubenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you briefly tell us what was discussed during that meeting, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we discussed -- I don't know how to put it. We discussed the situation on that day, we discussed our losses, the situation that prevailed after that, and obviously we mentioned civilians and detained members of the HVO who were brought at that moment. On my part, I mentioned the two wounded members of the HVO who were brought to my attention very late that day, and I've already mentioned that, with the knowledge of the battalion commander, I escorted one of those wounded to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in terms of these HVO soldiers, who suggested or decided, if anybody, that these were to be put into this room? Whose decision was that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. When you look at those situations realistically, when you look at the moment, anybody who had the right of deciding and who was of sound mind and was thinking rationally would have proposed that particular occasion for the accommodation of HVO members and civilians, given their huge number. There was no other, more appropriate room to accommodate that number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So again, whose decision was it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who was it who made that decision. However, my opinion is that the decision was the right one and appropriate, given the time and circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And are you now talking about putting the HVO people into that room or the civilians into the gym, or are these two separate events? I'm talking about that evening. Did you discuss both the HVO and the civilians, or only one of those two groups of people?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the decisions. I'm just sharing my opinion with you, because I was not part of the decision-making process. And I'm talking about both. And I underline, the situation was what it was, and given that situation and the availability of space, and given the necessity to provide security for both these groups, this was the right decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how many people, women and children, were put into the gym? Do you remember the number?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you the precise number. There were between 250 and 300 people in the gym, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where was the gym in relation to the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the same building. The building was the school. The battalion command was in the front part of the building and the gym was in a different part of the building. In any case, the two were in the same building, in the building of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I know that you said it was the right decision, given the, you know, the location, accommodation in these difficult times, but wasn't it dangerous to put so many people into the same area where the battalion command was working?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it was dangerous to accommodate so many people in the same place where the battalion command was, but the battalion command protected, or tried to provide security for these people. I'm looking at that situation from a practical situation and from the aspect that I have already discussed. Members of the battalion did whatever they could at the time, did everything, went out of our way to help these people and make them feel that they were not classical prisoners, because they were not. We tried to help them, protect them, provide security for them. And at the end of the day, they were protected by the civilian police. The battalion or the command battalion played a role that I've already described in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you think it was your duty to protect these civilians?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about the HVO persons. You said, I think, that the second day after they were accommodated, although I believe you said "detained" a moment ago, after they were accommodated in that room, who told you to visit that room? Bless you, my colleague.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion commander told me to do that. They were members of the military formation, and I, on my hand, was the most responsible in the military corps, and it was only logical for me to look at them and see what their situation was and if there were any proposals, I was duty-bound to share those with my commander. I may have mentioned the word "imprisonment" or -- but it may have been a slip of the tongue, because at that moment, I never -- I didn't see any bars on any of the windows. I did not consider these people to be classical detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But if one of these soldiers wanted to leave, could he do that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Where would they go?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Any place he chose. Back to his troops, for instance.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have expressed that wish to the International Red Cross, which granted that wish. Maybe they said that to the exchange commissions. When these events were taking place in the early days, I don't know where they could go, how could they have expressed a wish to go anywhere. There was nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sure you know what the mandate of the ICRC is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What are they doing in their normal course of action, and why did they come to a new area on that day? What's their mandate?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily to help resolve the situation at hand and to help people at the moment when they feel helpless and to deal with the problems of prisoners of war, of detainees, to help them with their further care. So I would say that their main -- their exclusive role is a humanitarian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Don't you agree with me that the purpose they came to your area -- I'm sorry. You want to say something?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that the purpose the ICRC was to come to your area was in fact to check what happened to these people, to fulfil what you described as their exclusive role? Wouldn't you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just wind up this part. You mentioned that two HVO soldiers were brought to you by ABiH soldiers, for you, to be treated, and you mentioned the name of one of these soldiers, and I believe you managed to bring him to the Zenica hospital. Do you remember the name of the second person, the second soldier?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. It was a long time ago. There were a lot of wounded people. My memory is rather good; however, on that day, I saw 69 wounded. It was a very strenuous, very long day. I'm not even sure whether this person that I escorted to Zenica, whether his name is -- was Zoran or Darko. I know that he was young, that he was seriously wounded. I already described what kind of wounds he had sustained. I thought it was normal for me to escort him, due to his condition. I tried to talk to him, but the only thing he asked me to do for him is to inform a member of the clergy. Maybe he hoped that that person would help him continue his Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond medical treatment somewhere in Croatia. I'm really not sure why. As for the other one, the one who was not so seriously wounded, I didn't know what to do with him, whether to find him a bed in the out-patients' clinic, in the school. But finally, I decided to send him to the gym. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell me the name of the hospital in Zenica you brought this person to?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is now called the Cantonal Hospital. It's the only hospital in Zenica. At that moment I believe that it was the clinical centre of Zenica. At that time, it was, and it still is, the only hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Dr. Ana, that's her first name or her last name, the doctor who --

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is her first name. She is a native of Kotor Varos. I came across her. I just happened to come across her and I asked her to help this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me turn back, still remain on the 8th of June, 1993, but turn back to what you testified yesterday. I believe you told us that sometime before the 8th of June, your battalion commander asked you to get prepared for possible combat operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I've already said that, in addition to the regular provocations and blockades of roads and shooting at different facilities, a few days before the 8th of June we received some alarming calls for help from the area of Velika Bukovica. In a certain way, the Muslim population there had already asked for our help because they had been attacked, there were provocations against them. There was even information that some 18 people had already been killed there. I believe that that is why my commander thought that there was a realistic danger of an imminent conflict, and accordance with that, he issued an order to be prepared. At the end of the day, it was war, and we were on the lines. Some of my men were on the Vlasic plateau, facing the Chetniks. So it was realistic to expect us to be prepared for anything that might happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you said that at a quarter past 4.00 in the morning on the 8th of June, 1993, you then received the first wounded person. And the order to get prepared from your battalion commander, you received the day before?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was issued a couple of days before. It was not a classical, written order. We were just told that we should be ready, that we should be prepared, and I acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the preparation, I believe, was, as you testified, together with your colleague Dr. Ribo, to have two reception centres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you. His name was Ribic, not Ribo. And it is correct. Considering the situation and the complexity of the terrain that we covered, in case their combat activities were stepped up, one reception centre, one triage centre, could not provide for the influx of possible wounded. That's why we decided to have two triage centres which were close to each other. This would service to provide for the most efficient assistance to any possible wounded that might come our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where were these two collection centres located?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mehurici. And the distance between the two of them was -- Mehurici is a small hamlet, a small village. There was an out-patient clinic which was in the centre, so to speak. And across the road from it was this reception, or triage centre on the ground floor of a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the first wounded which you received past 4.00 in the morning, where was he from? Where was he wounded?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the BiH army, of the 306th Mountain Brigade. I don't know exactly where he was wounded, but he arrived without his left or his right leg. One of his legs had been amputated. The second one who arrived, maybe half an hour later, also had sustained a wound from a land-mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on that day, 8th of June, 1993, there is information that more than 24 people were killed on that day, among them perhaps civilians. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I heard that only one or two days later. When I say "unfortunately," I'm sorry that these people were killed. I did hear about the incident involving detained members of the HVO, and I only learnt that a couple of days later. And yet a few days later, I learned that two of my wounded who had been brought too late were also there, that they were also in that execution line - I don't know what to call it- that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you asked to go somewhere to look at these bodies, for instance? Did somebody tell you that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one ever made such a request. I found out about this by chance, when in fact people guessed about what had happened, but no one ever officially requested me to go and have a look at those bodies, nor did I ever see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who told you about that later? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, assumptions were made about what had happened. I can't remember who told me that they had been killed. But there was this assumption that they had been killed, and I think that one of the soldiers told me about this. I really don't know who, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you talk about assumptions that they had been killed, what are you talking about? What kind of assumptions were made?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't making any assumptions, but I heard that they assumed that the people who had been arrested, who had been captured, had disappeared somewhere, and they assumed that the worst had happened to them. I didn't make any assumptions, but I heard about assumptions made by other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I mean, it's an obvious question, but do you think it's serious that more than 20 people were killed in the immediate surroundings of your location? Didn't you discuss that with your battalion commander within the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. It's not the duty of the battalion commander to talk to people at my level about such matters. I never spoke to him about that subject. He probably had contact with the services who were responsible for looking into such assumptions. He never spoke about the matter to me. I heard about this by chance, naturally. We heard that men had been captured, arrested, but he never spoke to me about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you hear about the survivors from this incident, massacre, if I can call it like that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, perhaps a few days later, or maybe even a month later, after the events, I found out that two wounded men who had been brought to me that evening, two members of the HVO, I heard that they had survived the massacre. I must be frank and say that I suspected that something particular had happened to the man who had been seriously wounded. There were a number of entry and exit wounds that he had and I couldn't understand how this had happened. But he was fairly agitated, and I didn't want to tire him, but later I found out that those two HVO members, those two wounded men, were involved in that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it possible that one of these persons was called Berislav Marijanovic, a Croat from the village of Paklarevo? Would that be a possibility? He was born in 1962.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. His name, I don't know whether it was Berislav. I think the first man was called Zoran or Darko. As for the second one, I really don't know what his name was. We considered him to be lightly wounded. We provided him with medical care. And given the situation, we placed him in the gym with the other civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you just said that something particular had happened to the man, and you were talking about a number of entry and exit wounds. Can you really be more specific about what you mean, what you saw?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a specific type of wound that can only be inflicted by the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond use of an automatic weapon. It can only be the result of a burst of fire, as far as I am familiar with such things. He had a number of wounds. The most critical wound was to the ribcage, on the right, and his ribs had been damaged. And he was a very seriously wounded man. As to the exact number of wounds that he had, I don't know how many there were exactly, but there were a number of wounds that indicated that he had been hit by a number of bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why was that special to you, as a doctor? Can you tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, they were brought to me very late. If you're referring to the arrival of those two HVO members. As far as the wounds are concerned, I believe that they must have been hit by a burst of fire. It wasn't the result of sniper fire. Someone had simply opened fire on the man at close range. And given the state of mind he was in, well, he seemed to be a textbook example of a wounded man who had been traumatised. And having arrived at our reception centre, he was already a little more stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if you are saying it was open -- there was open fire at a close range, that would suggest that it wasn't a part of a normal combat action, for instance. Is that what your assumptions or your assessment was at that time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, didn't you share that -- you may have answered, but please help me again. Didn't you share that with your commander, that you had a wounded soldier --

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told him, naturally. There was a report. I've already said that at the meeting, at around midnight, I don't know exactly when we had the meeting, but at that meeting I also reported on the case of the two HVO members who had been wounded, and I was requested to escort them to Zenica because of their wounds. But I didn't draw any conclusions as to where they had been wounded and how they had been wounded. All I did was establish the nature of the wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if you recall, what was the commander's response, if anything, when you told him that, during that late-night meeting?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what sort of measures were taken afterwards. In my opinion, I had done my bit. And later on, it wasn't for me to try and find out what had happened. About a month, a month and a half later, a friend of mine said that this young man was one of the men who had been shot at, who was a participant in this execution, was involved in this execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just finish this part. And again, you may have answered. You have never been requested to, by military police or civilian police or state police, to give an account of what had happened on the 8th of June, 1993 in relation to these soldiers you treated?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back to the 24th of April, 1993. And you described that you were called out, I believe, to go to a casualty of your troops. And then I believe you said outside Mehurici you came across an Arab who was wounded. Can you tell me, if you can recall after such a long time, what the wounds were? I believe you said they were complex wounds, but can you tell us perhaps the cause of these wounds?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was quite obvious that the wounds were gunshot wounds, that the two Arabs who were with him, and he was a third one, had weapons; they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us the location in relation to Mehurici where you came across these Arabs?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the exit from the village, there's a bridge that turns right, in the direction of Pilake [phoen] and it was at the exit by the bridge that I had stopped. I had the misfortune to be passing by at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So it was basically inside Mehurici that you came across the Arabs?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very exit from the village of Mehurici. It wasn't actually in the village itself. It was on the road leading out of the village, in the direction of Travnik and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it may consume some time, but if you could have a look at the map. I have a copy of a map. You, as a doctor, perhaps you can tell us -- just if you can circle the location with a pen. And for your convenience - I don't think it's disputed - I marked Mehurici with a yellow marker. If you could circle, pinpoint where you encountered this Arab.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't hear the witness now.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you can make a big circle around the area - it doesn't need to be precise - where you encountered this Arab.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the location. I can't see the road here. You only have the area around Mehurici, the villages. Fazlici is here, Mehurici here. It should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness just marked -- and perhaps you could make a circle around your dot.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] I can't be sure of this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that's sufficient. And the circle is between the villages of Poljanice and Fazlici, south of Mehurici. Thanks, Doctor. Let me go on -- just briefly on that document, you know, which you said -- basically said the document you found on this Arab which said he was a humanitarian worker from Egypt, signed by the minister, I believe, of interior of Croatia. Did you see other documentation like that while you were in that area or was that the only time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see a similar document. I found that document by chance, because I asked the other Arab, who knew some Serbo-Croat, I asked him to show me this passport. And it's only in that case that I saw what I mentioned. He was a humanitarian worker and he was to be granted free passage through territory in Croatia and territory under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that there may be time for a break. I think I only have a very few minutes left, so -- and I have a lot to cover, so I need to reorganise. If the break could be done perhaps now. I believe I may have another ten minutes, if my calculations are right. But I can go on if you want me to, and just finish it. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue for another ten minutes and we'll have our break at 20 to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us, Witness, and I'm continuing on the 24th of April, 1993, in that evening, I believe, when later the Emir came. But before he came, you said that you were sitting together and "six of us suggested" or "we suggested to go to the camp." It dealt with the release of these people who were detained or accommodated, whatever. "Six of us," you said, who were sitting together suggested to go to the camp.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say six of us. I said we who were there. I mentioned the commander, Mr. Ribo, and the other people who were there in addition to myself. I didn't mention a number. I didn't count them. At the time, that wasn't on my mind. A group of us decided to go up to the camp, that they relocated at a certain period of time later, they relocated the camp to a place called Poljanice. That's where they had a camp and we decided what we could do for the people up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Had you been before at the camp?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So why did you suggest to go to the camp?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was no other solution. They had taken the people there and parents and friends were affected. We didn't know what to do at the time. It seemed that we should go up there to try and find a Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond solution. Because we no longer saw any of the Arabs after that, after they had taken the civilians up there. Naturally, when we heard about how these people were humiliated, they had been chained, et cetera, well, it was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you and Ribo, you were sitting at the battalion command on that evening?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then I believe Ramadan went away, and then he came back with the Emir, as you described him?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before that, Ramadan turned up. Some of the -- one of the local Muslims must have told him about the situation. He then turned up. We tried to persuade him to help. At first he refused. He said it wasn't his affair. But later he agreed to help and then he turned up with Emir. And then only the battalion commander continued to negotiate with Emir. The rest of us didn't participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that Emir appeared escorted by armed members. How many armed members was Emir escorted by?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since it was night-time and -- well, there were two or three of them accompanying the Emir. They would turn up in their four-wheel-drives or Toyotas. Two or three appeared. They were armed Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And had you seen this Emir before or after this evening as well or was that the only time you had seen him?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd see them when they passed through Mehurici. I saw the Emir when he was passing through Mehurici, his vehicle. Since I said that they had a room up on the floor, the Emir would go to the room they had on the first floor. But I don't know what sort of work they did. I'd seen him before. I'd seen him passing by. But I never had direct contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in relation to that room they had, this office, you testified yesterday that after the Arabs left, they kept the room for a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm talking about. The Emir would go there occasionally. They held onto the room on the first floor of the school for a certain period of time afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember for how long they used, occupied the room?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Perhaps up until the time that the 27th was formed. That was in midsummer. Perhaps they were still using it then. I'm not quite sure what the purpose of this room was. But no army members went up to the floor, the first floor, where that room was located, not until the time when the 27th Brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And incidentally, when did you leave the area, Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I leave? On the 18th of March, 1996. The battalion command was located there, and later on, the brigade command was located there. I had duties to perform there, right up until the time that the wartime brigade was disbanded, right up until the time that we were to mobilise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So all the time you stayed in Mehurici as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The command was located in Mehurici, but given the intense fighting subsequently occurred. I didn't spend that much time in Mehurici. I was present in various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Our command was located up there. The unit's administrative section was located up there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me return in the final minutes to this Emir. Do you know his name? Do you remember what his name could be?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think the name of the person we're talking about right now was Wahiudin, but I'm not sure. Because I had very little contact with them. For professional reasons, I couldn't refuse to treat these two wounded men. But I tried to maintain my distance. I think his name was Wahiudin. Later, after Emir, Abu Haris appeared. I heard that he was an Emir and a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would there be Dr. Abu Haris?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was told, that this person was Dr. Abu Haris.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you say later he appeared, what do you mean by that? When did he appear? Later that evening?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that confused me too. In June, July, August, when everything had been hermetically sealed off, it was impossible to move and suddenly they appeared. I say "they appeared" because I would see them when they were passing by. I don't know exactly when he appeared, but it was perhaps sometime in mid-July. I can't be sure. I couldn't say exactly. But on the whole, they did appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But on that evening, the person who came with these armed people initiated by Ramadan, who talked to -- negotiated with your commander, that was not Abu Haris, in our opinion.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, his name was Wahiudin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe his appearance?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. He's a textbook example of a seasoned guerrilla. I think he had a scar. I think he had lost one eye, in fact. He had very evident scars. This was obviously a very seasoned guerrilla fighter. That's the impression he left given his arrogance and his refusal to have contact with our commander. He was a very difficult person. That was the impression I had. Naturally, later, when they remained alone and spoke to each other, I don't know how things unfolded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how old was he?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only make assumptions. It's difficult to assess their age, given their appearance, but I think he was between 30 and 40 years old at the time. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Had he facial hair?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all had beards, the ones I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us about Arabs you have seen. I believe the one person you mentioned was from Egypt. I believe you told us that Ramadan was from Syria.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Syria.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you remember other countries of origin of Arabs who were in your area?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I was speaking about the Arabs I was sure of, or rather, the Arabs whose names I could see in documents. In the case of this wounded man, I could see that he was from Egypt, at least on the basis of the passport he had. Ramadan told me that he was from Syria, but I don't know which other countries they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many Arabs did you treat while you were there? Was it the only time when you were treating this Arab you saw out of Mehurici, or were there other occasions?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, there was this Ramadan and the wounded Arab. Later they had their own doctor. I've already said that Abu Haris appeared. But even if they hadn't had their own doctor, after the events in Miletici, I considered them to be dogs of war. And to the extent that it was possible, I tried to avoid contact with them, not because I was afraid of them. And many members of my unit behaved in this way. I dealt with these two cases, and that was it, as far as the Arabs are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have two more questions which will take perhaps two or three minutes. Shall I deal with it now or do we want to make a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And with your permission, I would like to show a third exhibit to the witness, which has been prompted by something the witness said. And it's a previously admitted exhibit, DH128/6 -- 182, DH. And if the picture perhaps could be put onto the ELMO. It should speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before you do that, Witness: Your Honours, is that okay, that we show that to the witness? Because I haven't announced it. Thank you. If you can look at the picture, and perhaps check -- Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- that these persons, especially the person standing in front, obviously, of this white bus. Do you recognise anybody you know on this picture?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I recognise anybody. Maybe -- I assume that this person with the green beret could be Wahiudin. He has an eye patch and he's standing in front of the van. That might be him, but I can't be sure. I'm not sure whether it is him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the last question is: You just said after Miletici you considered these people - I believe you meant the Arabs - as dogs of war. Can you tell us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew from literature and from various books, as far as I have read about war, and judging by their behavior and by their arrogance, this guy, this Sheikh was a leader who made all the decisions. There was no military hierarchy. There was no military responsibility. When I arrived in Mehurici, they had already assumed a certain shape, the shape of a military unit. And especially after the brutal crime that they caused in Miletici, that's how I perceived them, as people without responsibility, without any discipline, without any proper hierarchy. All of them subject to the will of one man, without any real chain of command, without any real discipline. That's how I perceived them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a photo of a better quality. Maybe you can show that to the witness, to help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here is a colour photo, the same one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous one was also a colour photo. Mr. President, this is not helping me, because the person for whom I assume that I know him is turned away from the camera, and I can't see the scars that I could identify him by. I only assume, and only based on the scarf that he has around his neck, the Yasser Arafat type of scarf, the traditional scarf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. And I appreciate, by the way, the work you were doing as a doctor in these difficult times, helping these people down there. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. It is 10 to 4.00. We are going to resume at 20 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the break, I'm going to ask the Defence whether they have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. We don't have any additional questions for this witness. And the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just before the witness is released, I don't know whether you have any questions, Your Honours, but that you can sign his exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will have a few questions. Just a few minor things to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me clarify one thing. Do you have a degree in medicine or not, today?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I still have a few exams left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So you were a member of the medical corps and you're still a member of the medical corps, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A while ago, you were talking about the detainees. Actually, it was the Prosecution that mentioned the detainees, and the Defence objected to that term. I would like to be clear on that. The Judges have looked at the indictment, and in the indictment, it says that there was ill-treatment in the school, as well as in the blacksmith shop of Mehurici. In the indictment, and in the testimonies that we have heard, the witnesses of the Prosecution as well as of some witnesses of the Defence, have mentioned that they were either in the blacksmith shop or in the school. You were treating these persons, and the Judges would like to know whether these persons suffered any ill-treatment. You were there, you were present, you were treating these persons. You looked after them. You witnessed the facts. You were called as a Defence witness to help them with their case. As far as the ill-treatment of these persons is concerned, what can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, before you and the other Judges, I claim with full responsibility that what I saw there, what I witnessed there, was not ill-treatment. There was no inhumane treatment that might have put their people at risk. This did not take place, either in the school or in the blacksmith shop, as it is called. There was no torture, there was no ill-treatment. People were not deprived in any way. In my testimony, I have mentioned quite a few things showing how much we tried to help these people, to improve their conditions at the time. I know very well what prisons are and what torture is, what humiliation is, because at one point in time I suffered ill-treatment at the hands of the Serbian and Chetnik aggressor. And that's why I would like to underline that these people that you're asking me about, that both these groups were treated with a lot of tolerance and humanity, in a proper military way. These people who were in the gym were looked after. The civilian protection, and we provided logistical support only. In terms that I've already mentioned, we helped with food and other provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness who has testified here told us that there were about 25 children, more or less. As far as you can remember, did you see children in the Mehurici school? And I believe that there was even one very young child who could not have been more than a couple of weeks old. Do you remember that? Did you pay any attention to these children? Did you look after them?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember at the beginning of my testimony, when I was asked about the arrival of these people, I said that I noticed children in the group, and I suggested to the commander that our reserves of food were to be handed over to the civilian protection for the children and for the elderly. The children received three times a day milk and other things that were intended exclusively for children. And there were no cases of illness or lethal outcome among the children. As far as I can remember, one elderly person died, but he died because he was frail and old, and I believe that the conditions contributed to his death. But in any case, he died of natural causes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question. The Prosecution has asked you a while ago about the two persons who were seriously injured, whom you treated, and later on you learned that they belonged to a group of persons who were shot at. And the person that you treated, you said at the beginning that one of them was wounded in the leg, or his leg was missing, and that that person was a victim of an anti-personnel land-mine. What can you tell us about that? Because such an injury could not have originated from a land-mine.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, you're talking about the injured persons who were members of the BiH army, who were among the first to arrive after having been injured. They arrived there around a quarter past 4.00 in the morning. However, if you're referring to the HVO members whom I treated and who were seriously injured, none of them were injured by a land-mine. They both suffered gunshot injuries. One of them was seriously injured and the other one was slightly injured. The members of the BiH army who arrived amongst the first in the morning, they both suffered as a result of stepping on a land-mine, and they lost their legs as a result of that. I apologise for having to correct it. So which two men are you referring to? Are you referring to BiH army members or the HVO members? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The distinction has to be clear. You said that BiH army members were injured by land-mines. I remember that. And when you treated the wounded, did you wear a white uniform or did you wear a military uniform? How did you dress at the time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the triage centre, in the out-patients' clinic facilities, I wore a white coat and the insignia of the Red Cross. I insisted on that, with all my personnel, with the paramedics and the rest of my personnel. I told them that they should wear insignia of the Red Cross and bags with the Red Cross markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two HVO soldiers who were seriously injured, one of them was seriously injured and the other one was slightly injured, when they saw that you were a doctor, that you wore a white doctor's coat, did they talk to you about the circumstances of their wounding? Do you remember that episode? Did they talk to you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. I've already spoken about that. Given the number of wounded that we received on that day, the slightly wounded HVO soldier, once he was primarily treated, was moved to the gym, for a practical reason. We did have an out-patients' clinic, but it was overbooked, and the situation was such as it was at the moment. That's why we sent the slightly injured person to the gym. That's why I had not had much communication with him. I just took his case history and I sent him to the gym. The other one, I've already said that in addition to having been seriously injured, he was frightened. He was distracted. He was in a very bad psychological state. And while I was escorting him to Zenica, he only told me and asked me whether I could get him in touch with a priest. That was his only request and the only thing he told me. I suppose that he believed that a priest might be of assistance to him in further transportation. Members of the HVO at the time were sent for treatment to Croatia, Split and other places. I did not communicate much with him. However, I assumed that something specific must have happened, given the nature of his wounds, that looked like a burst of fire that he was exposed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he did not tell you anything about the circumstances of his wounding; he only asked for a priest, and that's all?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During that transportation, while we were escorting him to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I have two or three small questions on the HVO members who were in a place other than the gym. You called this room -- later on someone called this a blacksmith shop. That's the place I mean. If I have understood you well, you said before the break about this room or this place. It was not very comfortable. Is that a correct recollection of what you said?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is still my opinion. However, given the situation and the circumstances, the best solution was to send him there. Obviously, if we are talking about amenities and if you have a room which is 4 by 5 with 30 to 40 people there, obviously it was not comfortable and they did not have all the amenities, and it was not intended for so many people. That's what I meant when I said comfort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you how many people were in how much space and you have answered my question already before I was able to put it to you. You also --

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't answer. I said that there was a group of people, of some 15 people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, 15 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: First, what you said was translated as -- referred to 30 or 40 people, and then later on the interpreter corrects that and said 15 people. Could you again tell me how many people were in this place. I'm not clear now, I must say.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't 30 to 40. I didn't say that. There were 10 to 15 people, at the moment when I visited that room and when I entered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I also understood that you came there every day to check a patient who suffers from high blood pressure. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was my professional and ethical duty to keep an eye on that person in order to avoid any complications. We did not want his health to get worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... For some three to four weeks or maybe even more? I don't -- could you indicate me how long they were in this place?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know that they were kept sometime longer than those who were in the gym. I can't be sure of how much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you have or did they try to have with you conversations, or was it just to check your patients? Would you tell me something about your contacts with the group.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at them as patients, but I also looked at them as human beings, as individuals. I did talk to them. I don't know whether there is any time for me to tell you about a reward that I received from one of these people. This happened in 1995. I spoke to them. I tried to communicate with them, because I appreciated their situation. I understood what they were experiencing, because I had been in the same situation. And even if I hadn't been in such a situation, I thought it was normal to help these people, if with nothing else than with a kind word. And I believe it is only human and ethical to act like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us about this reward, this -- somebody who thanked you for having taken care of them during that period? Yes, can you share that with us.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person's name is Veso that is his nickname. His first name is probably Veselko. My family was expelled from Kotor Varos. My mother and my wife lived in Croatia until 1995. And when I went to Croatia in 1995 to bring them back, the bus stopped before Split and a person approached me in a restaurant. He asked me whether I remembered him. I said I did. And then he gave me a lift in his car to Zabok, where my family were, and he told me that whatever I needed, I could rely on him. He even offered me money. So it was a special satisfaction for me. It was a special thing for me to experience that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes, my last question: Did they talk to you about their physical condition, or was that a topic of discussion?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I asked them whether there were any problems, whether somebody was beating them. I tried to check them with my eyes to see if there were any bruises on their bodies and other signs of ill-treatment. What I could tell by inspecting them was that they hadn't been beaten. But they were depressed, just like any other person would be in their position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a couple of issues, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm just curious, Witness: What caused you to ask them whether they had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have used that word wrongly. I asked them what was the attitude of the civilian police towards them, because the civilian police were providing security for them. I also asked them whether there was anybody else who tried to approach them in order to beat them. It was war, and it was to be assumed that one thing or another could happen. At the end of the day, my task was to assess their complete physical situation, whether they suffered any ill-treatment. It was my task to inform my superior command if I noticed anything unusual on these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In answer to the question of Your Honour Swart, you said that the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond people in the blacksmith shop were kept a bit longer than the people in the gym. So let me ask you first: How long were the people in the gym kept?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. President asked me that. Oh, you're talking about the gym. I apologise. I believe that it was 10 to 14 days. I'm not sure. I can't be sure of that. But I believe that they were there some ten days or so. I really can't tell you any more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you remember: How many times in those 10 to 14 days did you, you personally, not somebody else, but just you, did you visit the gym in order to have contact with these people?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that immediately on their arrival, I informed the lady doctor who was with them about these people. There was a nurse there as well. So any further communication that I had was with the doctor. And if she needed something, if she indicated that there was something that she might need from our level, then I assisted her. Otherwise, I did not feel the need to enter the gym. Whatever I found important to know, I was told by the lady doctor who was with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So just so that I'm clear: How many times in these 10 to 14 days did you personally enter the gym?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Maybe four or five times, personally. I was always in the company of the lady doctor. I never entered on my own. I never entered the gym on my own. If there was a need for me to be there, I entered the gym with the lady doctor, and we visited the people together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And on each of these four to five occasions, how long, if you recall, would you have stayed inside the gym?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that important? I really can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him -- put the question. The answer is in your favour, so proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It depended. Sometimes I would stay a few minutes. I never stayed longer than ten minutes in the gym. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And let me go to the blacksmith shop. In these, a little bit more than 10 to 14 days, how many times did you enter the blacksmith shop?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, how many times? Throughout the entire period, you mean, while they were there? Maybe five or six times. Just to see this person who had high blood pressure and to check his overall health condition. But every time I entered the blacksmith shop, I was accompanied by a civilian policeman or anybody else who provided security. So I just want to say that in order to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why would this person provide security?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not so much providing security. I did not feel that I should have bodyguards. It was just the case of this person providing security being responsible, having responsibility towards his superiors, and I came in my capacity as a doctor, as a person who was there to help patients. I just wanted to make sure that everybody knew that I didn't go there to do something else, which was not my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now give the floor to Defence counsel so that they can put questions to the witness that arise out of the questions asked by the Chamber and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you examined the HVO member, when you were treating him, you said that you contacted your commander to obtain authorisation to accompany him as far as Zenica. Could you please tell us what you said to the commander on that occasion. What explanation did you give him for wanting to escort the wounded man?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that this man was seriously wounded and it was essential to accompany him. It was essential to escort him. I told him that he was an HVO member and that he required further medical treatment in hospital, given the nature of his wounds, given the state he was in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menzil, was this your task, as a doctor, was it your task to inform the commander the reason for which you wanted to escort a wounded man, whether the wounded man was a member of the HVO or the ABiH? Were there medical reasons for making such requests?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course there were medical reasons, but yesterday I said that I had to -- two words I had made, one to the ABiH and the other was the Hippocratic Oath. I had to inform the commander of the situation and ask him to authorise me to accompany the wounded man, given the state the wounded man was in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned from Zenica and you attended a meeting at around midnight, it was a meeting that was attended by a part of the command. As head of the medical corps, was it your duty to provide information of a medical kind to the commander and tell the members of the command, in relation to what had happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. And I provided such information. I presented the facts. I informed them about what had happened that day and heard about other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is on its feet. I'll give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Observation that arises out of cross-examination and Defence choose not to re-examine and not out of Judges' questions, that conversation late at night, midnight. But the witness answered already.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have concluded that part, but I do believe that the Judges asked about the wounds sustained by this HVO member. That's why I put the question to the witness. I only have one other question, which is -- which arises from the additional questions put to the witness by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you entered the gym with the lady doctor on a number of occasions, and my question is: Did the doctor at any point in time tell you that there was a problem that concerned the maltreatment of children or the elderly, of other people who were kept in that sports hall?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this concludes your testimony. You have answered all the questions put to you by the Defence, by the Prosecution. You will have to sign a document before you leave. Before I ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, I'd be grateful if you could write down your name and today's date on the map. This is necessary in order to identify the document. Your name and the date must be noted. It's the 13th of January, 2005 today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will show the document to the Prosecution, to Defence counsel, to the accused, and to the Judges. The registrar will take charge of the document. I assume that the Prosecution would like to have it admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the number for this document will be 949 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have just observed the admission into evidence of this document which you have signed and on which you have written down the date. Thank you for having come to The Hague. Thank you for having testified here, for having answered all the questions. So we wish you a good trip home and we wish you all the best and hope that you will obtain your degree soon in the future. I'll now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have another witness for today?
